title: Why Lilienthal Strapped a Parachute to His Glider
topic: Why the German engineer Otto Lilienthal attached a parachute to his glider (Berlin, 1895)

lines: A German engineer strapped a parachute to a glider that kept diving.
Berlin, 1895. Otto Lilienthal was already called the flying man.
His glider had a habit of pitching down.
He flew it by shifting his body, like modern hang gliders.
But when the glider pointed at the ground, he could not shift enough.
He built a tower shed on a Berlin hill and jumped from its roof.
He tried many ways to make the glider steadier.
He and his brother Gustav made more than two thousand flights.
His total time in the air was five hours.
You see, a parachute is like a hand pushing back against your fall.
The real reason was his glider could dive faster than he could correct it.
A parachute creates drag, the force that slows a falling object.
Lilienthal attached one to the glider, to slow his fall if it stalled.
One year later, his glider stalled again.
He fell from the glider, broke his neck, and died the next day.
The engineer who tried to survive a stall died in a stall.

claims.claim: Lilienthal's gliders were difficult to manoeuvre and had a tendency to pitch down, and he had previously struggled to recover because the glider relied on weight shift, which was difficult to achieve when pointed at the ground.
Lilienthal controlled his gliders by changing the centre of gravity by shifting his body, much like modern hang gliders.
His training area in 1892 was the Maihoehe hill in Steglitz, Berlin, where he built a 4-metre-high shed in the shape of a tower to obtain a jumping-off place 10 metres high.
Working with his brother Gustav, Lilienthal made over 2,000 flights in gliders of his design, with a total flying time of five hours.
On 9 August 1896, Lilienthal's glider stalled and he was unable to regain control; falling from about 15 metres, he broke his neck and died the next day.
A parachute is a device designed to slow an object's descent through an atmosphere by creating drag or aerodynamic lift.
Parachute flight dynamics involve deployment, inflation and steady descent, with flight characteristics determined by inertia and aerodynamic drag.
Hang gliders such as Lilienthal's were among the pioneering aircraft of the 1890-1930 era that preceded the rebirth of hang gliding and ultralight sport aviation.
